persona.who: 21, Indian-American senior at Rutgers, born in NJ. Parents from Gujarat. Dating a white classmate; hasn't told parents. Feels neither fully Indian nor American.
persona.note: my parents keep asking when I'll 'settle down with a nice Gujarati boy' and I've been with my boyfriend for 2 years and he's not Indian. I feel like whichever way I go I lose a part of me

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call being seen as less than you are, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise being asked to choose, and the fear that either choice will cost you a part of yourself.

understanding.core_struggle: A young woman is being asked by her parents to choose between a 'nice boy' and the non-Indian partner she has been with for two years, and she fears losing herself either way.
understanding.mirror: You are being asked to choose, and whichever way you go, you feel you will lose a part of yourself.
understanding.insight: You are not asking for too much. You are being handed a smaller picture of yourself than the one you live, and the smallness is theirs.
understanding.mechanism_label: Being seen as less than you are

queries.hook: Being asked to choose between the family you were born into and the life you have built, and the fear that either choice will cost you a part of yourself.
queries.diagnose: When others see only a role or a picture, their picture is their smallness and not your measure; the harm deepens only when their picture begins to replace your own.
queries.steady: What you are cannot be cut smaller by what they see; your worth was never theirs to grant, and standing in your own truth is itself the duty.
queries.act: Speak the true thing gently and firmly, hold your ground on what is yours, and do your own duty without shrinking to fit the picture they hold.
queries.story: A woman of learning and standing, dismissed by her husband's family, who questioned them openly and stood in her truth until they had no answer.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥
verse.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Not 'stick to the role you were born into'. It's about honest fit with your own nature, not caste or family script.

matched.label: My parents' expectations weigh on me

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Krishna is telling Arjuna that it is better to follow your own nature, even if you stumble, than to copy another person's path perfectly. Doing the work that fits who you are, with all its flaws, does not lead to any fault or harm. You are being asked to choose between a path laid out by your parents and the one you have walked with your partner. Either choice feels like it will cost you a piece of who you are.
verse.for_you: The choice your parents are forcing on you is a trap. Their path is not your own. Walk the path you have built with your partner, even if they call it imperfect. It is the only one that is truly yours.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Right after naming the five causes of any action, Krishna warns about the person who ignores four of them.
verse.sanskrit: तत्रैवं सति कर्तारमात्मानं केवलं तु यः । पश्यत्यकृतबुद्धित्वान्न स पश्यति दुर्मतिः ॥
verse.line: If you think you alone made it happen, or alone made it fail, you're not seeing the whole picture.
verse.translation: That being so, whoever, through an untrained understanding, sees himself alone as the doer does not truly see.
verse.why: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.
verse.misuse: Not a way to dodge responsibility; you are still one of the five causes.

prasang.title: What makes an action happen
prasang.summary: Every action has five causes: the setting, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and providence. Seeing oneself as the only doer is a mistake.
prasang.lesson: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.

verse.meaning: Krishna explains that every action has five causes: the setting, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and providence. He warns that if you think you alone are the doer and the sole maker of success or failure, you are not seeing the whole picture. You are only one part of a larger web, not the entire cause of the outcome.
verse.for_you: Yesterday's verse named the grip of their choice. Today, see that your parents are only one cause in your life's web. They are not the whole picture, and you are not the whole cause of their happiness or their loss.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Queen Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She tells him not to hold himself in contempt or settle for too little. She urges him to set his mind on what is truly good and to stop being afraid. She reminds him that those who never try never succeed, and that past failure does not have to define him.
verse.for_you: You have already built a life and a partnership. Do not let their fear of loss shrink your sense of who you are. Set your mind on what is truly good for you, and do not be afraid of the fight ahead.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
verse.sanskrit: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
verse.line: You are pure awareness, wider than any worry. Don't let your mind shrink into pettiness.
verse.translation: This whole universe is pervaded by you and strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness; do not fall into smallness of mind.
verse.why: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

prasang.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.story_hook: A powerful king bowed before a boy whose body was bent in eight places, and asked him how to be free.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free. Ashtavakra answers that this whole universe is strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness, so do not fall into smallness of mind. The king is being told that freedom is not a prize to win but the way he already sees himself, wider than any worry or role.
verse.for_you: Yesterday's verse named the grip. Today it names what holds it. When your parents shrink your life to a choice, remember you are the awareness that watches the choice. You are the whole room, not just the corner they put you in.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse.sanskrit: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥
verse.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.
verse.why: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.
verse.misuse: Kind speech doesn't mean avoiding hard truths; it means saying them without cruelty.

prasang.title: Three kinds of food, offering, austerity and giving
prasang.summary: Food, offering, austerity and giving each come in three kinds. Speech should be true, kind and helpful; giving should expect nothing back; effort for show doesn't last.
prasang.lesson: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that the discipline of speech is to use words that cause no distress, that are true, pleasant and beneficial. It is not about hiding, but about saying what is real without wounding. This is the standard for how we meet each other.
verse.for_you: Your parents are asking for a yes or no, but your voice can hold the whole truth. Tell them what you feel without cruelty, and let them hear it. Your part is the truth, not the outcome.

verse.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
verse.setting: Brihaspati counsels Indra on how to hold authority among difficult people.
verse.sanskrit: मृदुमप्यवमन्यन्ते तीक्ष्णादुद्विजते जनः / मातीक्ष्णो मा मृदुर्भूस्त्वं तीक्ष्णो भव मृदुर्भव
verse.line: People walk over the soft and fear the harsh. Be firm when it's needed, gentle when it's needed.
verse.translation: People look down even on the gentle, and they shrink from the harsh. Do not be only harsh, do not be only soft: be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is.
verse.misuse: Firmness here means clarity, not cruelty.

matched.label: I need to set boundaries with family

verse.meaning: Brihaspati tells Indra that people walk over the soft and shrink from the harsh. The answer is not to be only one or the other. Be firm when firmness is needed, gentle when gentleness is. This is how a leader holds space for truth without breaking the people in it.
verse.for_you: You do not have to be the nice girl or the rebel. You can be firm about your life and gentle about your love. Let them see the boundary clearly, and let them feel your care at the same time.

story.title: Parvati holds to her choice
story.story_hook: The sages came to talk Parvati out of it, and they listed every flaw in the man she had chosen.
story.summary: Reborn as Parvati, Sati resolves to marry Shiva and spends years in austerity. The seven sages come to test her, mocking Shiva as a homeless ascetic and offering her a better match. She answers that gold keeps its nature even in fire, and that the heart wants the one it has chosen.
story.lesson: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.

anchor.speaker: Parvati
anchor.setting: Parvati answers the sages who mock her resolve to win Shiva through years of austerity.
anchor.sanskrit: सत्य कहेहु गिरिभव तनु एहा। हठ न छूट छूटै बरु देहा॥ कनकउ पुनि पषान तें होई। जारेहुँ सहजु न परिहर सोई ॥
anchor.line: Gold comes from stone, and even in fire it stays gold. Hold to what you are.
anchor.translation: You speak truly: this body was born of a mountain, so its resolve will not break, even if the body does. Gold too is born of stone, and even in fire it does not give up its nature.
anchor.why: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.
anchor.misuse: Steadiness is not stubbornness; keep checking that the goal is still worth it.

prasang.title: Parvati holds to her choice
prasang.summary: Reborn as Parvati, Sati resolves to marry Shiva and spends years in austerity. The seven sages come to test her, mocking Shiva as a homeless ascetic and offering her a better match. She answers that gold keeps its nature even in fire, and that the heart wants the one it has chosen.
prasang.story_hook: The sages came to talk Parvati out of it, and they listed every flaw in the man she had chosen.
prasang.lesson: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.

story.hook_title: The sages listed every flaw in the man Parvati had chosen
story.teaser: The sages listed every flaw in the man Parvati had chosen
story.for_you: Your parents are offering you a safer match. But you are the gold. Let your choice for who you love stay gold even in the fire of their anger, and hold to what you are.

script: You are caught between two worlds right now. You are studying, building your life, and your parents are telling you to choose a nice boy. They want you to walk a path they laid out. You are afraid that either choice will cost you a piece of who you are.
Arjuna is standing on the battlefield. He is terrified and confused. He tells Krishna that he does not know what is right. He asks what he should do. And Krishna replies:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्, स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम्.
In plain words: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.

Krishna says that it is better to follow your own nature, even if you stumble, than to copy another person's path perfectly. Doing the work that fits who you are, with all its flaws, does not lead to any fault or harm. This is easier said than done, because your parents want you to be safe and happy. But their idea of safety is not your own. The truth is that no path is perfect. The only way to avoid a deeper loss is to do the work that fits you.

Your parents are asking you to be someone smaller than the person you are becoming. Their path is not your own. The work you have done with your partner is your own. Walk that path. It is the only one that is truly yours.
What is the work that fits who you are today?

depth.life: You are caught between two worlds. Your parents want you to choose a safe path, but you have already built a life with your partner over two years. They see your choice as imperfect, but it is the one you know. You keep fighting because you are being asked to shrink yourself to fit their idea of you.
depth.points: The verse says to do your own work, even if it is flawed, rather than doing someone else's work perfectly. It is about finding your true fit, not about following a family script. Your life with your partner is your own duty, and that is what matters.
depth.practice: Write down one thing you value about your relationship that your parents do not see. Read it once before you talk to them.
depth.question: What does your own path look like when you are not trying to make it perfect?
